variants.title: Follow a write to disk
variants.context: An LSM tree records a write durably first, keeps a sorted working set in memory, flushes it as an immutable SSTable, and merges files in the background. The newest visible version of each key must win.
variants.prompt: A client updates a key. Put the storage engine’s steps in order.

items.text: Freeze the full MemTable and flush it as a new SSTable, published atomically.
Append the record and checksum to the write-ahead log.
Insert the newest version into the sorted MemTable.
Compact runs in the background, keeping the newest visible version.

variants.hint: Durability comes before anything the engine could lose on a crash.
variants.explanation: WAL → MemTable → flush → compact. If an acknowledged record existed only in memory, a crash would lose it.

variants.title: Follow a write to disk
variants.context: An LSM tree records a write durably first, keeps a sorted working set in memory, flushes it as an immutable SSTable, and merges files in the background. The newest visible version of each key must win.
variants.prompt: A delete arrives for a key. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Merge files later, retaining the tombstone until its safety boundary passes.
Flush the frozen MemTable into an immutable file with index and footer.
Append the tombstone to the WAL before acknowledging.
Insert the tombstone into the MemTable so reads see the deletion now.

variants.hint: A delete is written like any other record; it just carries a tombstone.
variants.explanation: Same path as an update. The tombstone must survive compaction until no older value can reappear from any file, replica, or restore.

variants.title: Follow a write to disk
variants.context: An LSM tree records a write durably first, keeps a sorted working set in memory, flushes it as an immutable SSTable, and merges files in the background. The newest visible version of each key must win.
variants.prompt: Many small random writes arrive. Put the steps that turn them into sequential file writes in order.

items.text: Keep the newest versions sorted in memory.
Merge selected runs into verified outputs and replace the inputs.
Record each write durably in the append-only WAL.
Stream the frozen sorted set into blocks and publish one immutable SSTable.

variants.hint: Random updates become sequential because the engine never edits a file in place.
variants.explanation: Append, sort in memory, flush sequentially, compact. No existing data page is ever rewritten in place.

variants.title: Narrow a point lookup
variants.context: A point lookup checks mutable memory, then immutable memory, then on-disk runs from newest to oldest. Each stage can remove work, but only a value or tombstone at the newest visible sequence decides the answer.
variants.prompt: A reader asks for one exact key. Put the lookup stages in order.

items.text: Skip files whose key interval or Bloom filter proves the key cannot be there.
Verify and decompress that block, then search its sorted records.
Search the current and frozen MemTables; a match outranks every file.
Binary-search the sparse index for the block that could hold the key.

variants.hint: Memory holds the newest versions, so it is checked before any file.
variants.explanation: Memory → file pruning → sparse index → data block. Each stage removes work; the last one finds the newest visible version or a tombstone.

variants.title: Narrow a point lookup
variants.context: A point lookup checks mutable memory, then immutable memory, then on-disk runs from newest to oldest. Each stage can remove work, but only a value or tombstone at the newest visible sequence decides the answer.
variants.prompt: A key was overwritten a minute ago and the new version is still in memory. Put the lookup stages in order.

items.text: Only then would it use the index and read a data block.
Stop: a memory match outranks every older SSTable.
Check mutable memory first and find the newest version there.
Only on a miss would the reader prune files by interval and Bloom filter.

variants.hint: The newest version wins, and it lives in memory.
variants.explanation: The lookup ends at the first stage. Older versions on disk are never consulted because memory already holds the newest visible value.

variants.title: Narrow a point lookup
variants.context: A point lookup checks mutable memory, then immutable memory, then on-disk runs from newest to oldest. Each stage can remove work, but only a value or tombstone at the newest visible sequence decides the answer.
variants.prompt: A key that was never written is requested. Put the lookup stages in order.

items.text: Consult the sparse index only for files with a positive filter result.
Read and verify a candidate block only when the index points to one.
Check the MemTables and find nothing.
Reject every file whose Bloom filter returns negative.

variants.hint: A negative Bloom result proves absence; a positive one only permits a look.
variants.explanation: For a true miss, most files are rejected by their filters. Only false positives cost an index lookup and a block read.

variants.title: Read the Bloom filter
variants.context: A Bloom filter proves that an exact key is absent from a file. A positive result means only “possibly present”, so the read continues through the sparse index and data block.
variants.prompt: A file’s Bloom filter returns “possibly present” for the key. What should the reader do?
options: Continue through the sparse index to the data block.
Return the value the filter is holding for that key.
Skip the file, because the filter was not certain.
optionFeedback: A positive result is a permission to look, not an answer.
A Bloom filter stores no values; it can only answer membership.
Skipping on a positive could miss a real value or tombstone.
variants.hint: Which result is a proof, and which is only a hint?
variants.explanation: Bloom filters prove absence. A positive result may be a false positive, so the reader must still consult the index and the block.

variants.title: Read the Bloom filter
variants.context: A Bloom filter proves that an exact key is absent from a file. A positive result means only “possibly present”, so the read continues through the sparse index and data block.
variants.prompt: A range scan needs every key between two bounds. Can the point-key Bloom filter reject a file for the scan?
options: No. The filter answers exact keys, not intervals.
Yes, provided the filter is large enough.
Yes, by testing the two bounds of the range.
optionFeedback: A filter built on exact keys cannot say whether any key inside an interval exists.
Size changes the false-positive rate; it does not change what the filter can answer.
Testing two endpoints says nothing about the keys between them.
variants.hint: What question was the filter built to answer?
variants.explanation: A point-key Bloom filter cannot reject an interval. Range scans depend on compaction layout, key-range overlap, block size, and readahead.

variants.title: Read the Bloom filter
variants.context: A Bloom filter proves that an exact key is absent from a file. A positive result means only “possibly present”, so the read continues through the sparse index and data block.
variants.prompt: A Bloom filter returns negative for a key, but the engine still reads the file’s index. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: negatives must always be double-checked.
The filter must be rebuilt from the memory snapshot.
Wasted work: a negative proves the key is absent.
optionFeedback: Only positives need confirmation; negatives are certain.
Filters are derived from the records committed to the file, so the negative is correct.
A negative Bloom result is a guarantee; reading the file cannot find the key.
variants.hint: Only one of the two answers can be wrong. Which one?
variants.explanation: A negative means the key is definitely not in the file. Consulting the index anyway spends I/O for nothing.

variants.title: Measure write amplification
variants.context: Compaction rewrites data to keep reads cheap. Write amplification is total bytes the device writes divided by logical bytes the application wrote.
variants.prompt: The application writes 100 GB of logical data per day. Flushes and compaction bring total device writes to 800 GB per day. What is the write amplification?
variants.hint: Divide total device writes by logical writes.
variants.explanation: 800 ÷ 100 = 8. Every logical byte is rewritten about eight times over its life, which costs bandwidth and device endurance.

mistakes.feedback: Amplification is a ratio, not a difference: 800 ÷ 100.
Divide device writes by logical writes, not the other way around.

variants.title: Measure write amplification
variants.context: Compaction rewrites data to keep reads cheap. Write amplification is total bytes the device writes divided by logical bytes the application wrote.
variants.prompt: The application writes 50 GB per day. The device writes 350 GB per day in total. What is the write amplification?
variants.hint: Divide total device writes by logical writes.
variants.explanation: 350 ÷ 50 = 7. Leveled compaction often lands in this range because values move through several levels.

mistakes.feedback: Subtracting gives extra bytes, not the amplification ratio.
Divide device writes by logical writes.

variants.title: Measure write amplification
variants.context: Compaction rewrites data to keep reads cheap. Write amplification is total bytes the device writes divided by logical bytes the application wrote.
variants.prompt: A device can sustain 600 GB of writes per day. Write amplification is measured at 12. What is the most logical data the application can write per day without exceeding the device?
variants.hint: Logical writes × amplification must stay within the device budget.
variants.explanation: 600 ÷ 12 = 50 GB of logical writes per day. Reserve part of that budget for reads, WAL syncs, repair, and backups.

mistakes.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing; the device would write 12 times the logical volume.
The device budget includes all rewrites, not just logical data.

variants.title: Choose the compaction rule
variants.context: Compaction merges immutable runs, keeps the newest version, and drops tombstones only after their safety boundary. Size-tiered favors sustained ingest; leveled favors predictable reads at the cost of rewrites.
variants.prompt: Point reads are latency-critical, disks have spare write bandwidth, and the key space is updated evenly. Which strategy fits?
options: Leveled compaction: fewer overlapping runs per read.
Size-tiered compaction: fewer rewrites, more overlap.
No compaction: keep every flushed file in place.
optionFeedback: Leveled keeps non-overlapping ranges in larger levels, so a read touches fewer runs.
Size-tiered leaves more overlapping files, which raises read amplification.
Without compaction, run count and read amplification grow without bound.
variants.hint: Which resource is scarce here: read latency or write bandwidth?
variants.explanation: When reads must be predictable and rewrite bandwidth is available, leveled compaction spends writes to buy a smaller read shape.

variants.title: Choose the compaction rule
variants.context: Compaction merges immutable runs, keeps the newest version, and drops tombstones only after their safety boundary. Size-tiered favors sustained ingest; leveled favors predictable reads at the cost of rewrites.
variants.prompt: A crash interrupts a compaction halfway through writing its output. What must be true for recovery to be safe?
options: The WAL was discarded once compaction started.
The inputs stayed until the output was durable.
The output was published block by block as written.
optionFeedback: The WAL protects unflushed writes and must outlive every file it covers.
If inputs remain, the interrupted merge can restart from the prior state.
Publishing partial output would let restart trust an incomplete file.
variants.hint: Immutability means nothing is repaired in place. What stays available until the new file is proven?
variants.explanation: Compaction never edits inputs; it replaces them only after the verified output is atomically referenced. Until then, the old files are the truth.

variants.title: Choose the compaction rule
variants.context: Compaction merges immutable runs, keeps the newest version, and drops tombstones only after their safety boundary. Size-tiered favors sustained ingest; leveled favors predictable reads at the cost of rewrites.
variants.prompt: To reclaim space, an operator drops tombstones older than a day. Deleted rows later reappear. What happened?
options: Tombstones cannot be compacted away at all.
The Bloom filter reported the key as absent.
It was purged while older values still survived.
optionFeedback: Tombstones can be dropped, but only after the safety boundary passes.
A filter cannot resurrect data; only a surviving older version can.
A tombstone needs a proof boundary, and age alone is not that proof.
variants.hint: What does a tombstone protect against, and for how long?
variants.explanation: A tombstone can be discarded only after the system knows no older value can reappear. Removing it because it is old resurrects deleted data.
